paras: The lynching of Bob Bryant and Will Morris took place before daylight on Sunday, May 3, 1903, when a crowd of armed farmers took the two Black prisoners from sheriff's deputies and hanged them from the Yazoo bridge at Haynes Bluff, near Vicksburg, Mississippi. The men were accused of shooting the planter W. H. Legg, and Bryant was said to have confessed. Within two days dispatches reported that Morris's rope had broken and that he had escaped, a story a Mississippi paper later called untrue.

According to a Vicksburg special to the New Orleans States, William Legg, a planter at Adams' Landing west of Redwood, went to a burning gin house on the night of May 1 and was "shot down in cold blood" by Black men. The Washington Times gave a fuller version: the accused had planned to rob Legg's store, set his cotton gin on fire, and shot him when he returned to the store, which he had left open.

Posses from Redwood, Oak Ridge and Adams county hunted for three suspects, and the first dispatch predicted that "a wholesale lynching" would follow if they were caught. By the evening of May 2, Bob Bryant, described as a former tenant on the Legg place, had been captured and had confessed to the posse, accusing a second man, Will Morris, of firing the fatal shot.

At 11 o'clock that night Deputy Sheriff Frank Scott and four other deputies set out for town with the prisoners. About 400 yards south of the Legg place, some 200 farmers armed with rifles and shotguns stopped them and demanded the prisoners. Scott pleaded that the law be allowed to take its course, but the mob's leaders gave the deputies a choice between surrendering the men and "sacrificing their own lives in a useless resistance," and the crowd took the two men into a nearby thicket.

The bodies were reported found hanging from the bridge on Sunday morning. The St. Louis Republic's correspondent placed the hanging at a bridge on a public road three miles from Redwood and said there was "not a shot fired from the orderly crowd."

On May 4, a party visiting the bridge reportedly found that Morris's rope had broken when he was pushed off and that he had fallen into shallow water. His shoes and the noose were found about 100 yards below the bridge, with bare footprints leading toward the swamp, and a posse was said to be searching for him.
No report of Morris's recapture, an inquest, or any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage found.

White papers across the country ran the Vicksburg wire on May 4 and in weeklies into the next week, calling the prisoners "the assassins of W. H. Legg" and stating that "Robbery was the motive." The Savannah Morning News headed it "WITH THEIR LIVES NEGRO ASSASSINS PAID THE PENALTY FOR THEIR CRIME," while the New Haven Journal and Courier wrote "Mississippi Mob Takes the Law in Its Own Hands."

The St. Louis Republic and the Washington Times described the mob as "the best citizens" of the area. In Mississippi, the Hattiesburg Daily Progress called it "the first lynching of the year" in the delta and wrote that the friends of the dead man "did not have the patience to wait the slow progress of the law." The same paper treated the escape story as "A rather funny thing" and then, on May 11, dismissed it as a correspondent's invention.

The Worcester Spy, by contrast, said in an editorial titled "MORE MOB VIOLENCE" that there was not "the slightest excuse for lynching" since the authorities were proceeding under the law. July lists of "Mob Law" counted "Two negroes hanged, Payne's Bluff, Miss., May 4." The only Black-press notice found is a one-line entry under May 2 in the Chicago Broad Ax's year-end chronology for 1903.

Accounts differ on whether Morris died: the first wire reported both bodies hanging from the bridge, while dispatches from May 4 to 6 said he had survived the fall. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress later asserted that the escape had been "proved" false but named no source.

reader.title: Lynching of Bob Bryant and Will Morris
bases: Two Black prisoners accused of murdering a planter were taken from deputies by an armed crowd of farmers and hanged from a bridge (A5, A8, A15).

Every report has at least Bryant hanged dead by a mob of farmers, given as 200 (A5, A16), who took the prisoners from deputies over their protest, and a Mississippi paper said the friends of the murdered man would not wait for 'the slow progress of the law' (A17); whether Morris also died is disputed (A15, A28).

Three independently sourced dispatches from Vicksburg (the general wire, A5; the St. Louis Republic's special, A8; the Washington Times, A9) agree that both prisoners were taken and hanged from a bridge; only the death of the second man is disputed (A15, A16, A28).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Vicksburg wire calling the men 'the assassins of W. H. Legg', under headlines such as 'WITH THEIR LIVES NEGRO ASSASSINS PAID THE PENALTY FOR THEIR CRIME' and '200 ANGRY MEN HANG TWO NEGROES TO YAZOO BRIDGE'.
The St. Louis Republic described an 'orderly crowd' of 'the best citizens' and said the two 'expatiated their crime'.

The Hattiesburg Daily Progress said the men 'without any doubt would have been legally executed' but the friends of the dead man lacked patience, then joked about the escape and later called it a lie.
The Worcester Spy's 'MORE MOB VIOLENCE' said there was not 'the slightest excuse for lynching' since authorities were proceeding legally.
The New Haven Journal and Courier headed the wire 'Mississippi Mob Takes the Law in Its Own Hands', and July lists counted it among thirteen cases of 'Mob Law'.
The Chicago Broad Ax's year-end chronology recorded the names, place and the accusation in one line.

conflicts.note: The escape reports are later and give physical detail (shoes, noose, footprints) but come from the lynchers' neighborhood; the Hattiesburg denial gives no source. No report of Morris's recapture or death was found.
The 2000 figure appears only in a weekly digest and is likely a misprint of the wire's 200.
The dated Vicksburg dispatches of May 3 are the best evidence; May 2 is the date of the shooting.
